en: Udāna 5.5 Uposatha Sutta Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, in the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother.
Now on that occasion—the Uposatha day—the Blessed One was seated surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

Then, when the night had advanced and the first watch had passed, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms in reverential salutation toward the Blessed One, and said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, the night has advanced; the first watch has passed; the Saṅgha of bhikkhus has been sitting for a long time.
May the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha to the bhikkhus.
When this was said, the Blessed One remained silent.

A second time, when the night had advanced and the middle watch had passed, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, and said this to the Blessed One:
“The night has advanced, Bhante; the middle watch has passed; the Saṅgha of bhikkhus has been sitting for a long time.
May the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha to the bhikkhus.”
A second time, the Blessed One remained silent.
A third time, when the night was far spent, in the final watch, at the rising of the dawn,
at the face of the joyous night, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and approached the Blessed One.
Having extended his joined palms in reverential salutation, he said this to the Blessed One:
“The night has passed, Bhante; the final watch has ended; the dawn has risen; the night has a joyful face; the community of monks has been seated for a long time.
May the Blessed One, Bhante, recite the Pātimokkha to the monks.”
“Ānanda, the assembly is not pure.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
“With reference to which person did the Blessed One say this?”
“‘The assembly, Ānanda, is not pure,’ [he said].
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, encompassing the entire Saṅgha of bhikkhus with his mind, directed his attention to their minds.
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna saw that person who was immoral, of evil character, impure, and of suspect conduct.”
Seeing a person of concealed conduct, who is not a recluse though claiming to be a recluse, who does not live the holy life though claiming to live the holy life—
one who is internally rotten, leaking, and putrid— sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus,
he rose from his seat, approached that person, and having approached, said this to him:
“Arise, friend! You have been seen by the Blessed One;
you no longer have communion with the bhikkhus.
When this was said, that person remained silent.
A second time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this to that person:
“Arise, friend! You have been seen by the Blessed One;
you have no further association with the bhikkhus.”
A second time...
and a third time, that person remained silent.

Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, taking that person by the arm, led him out through the outer gate, gave him the needle-and-cord [for punishment], and approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, that person has been expelled by me.
The assembly is pure.
Let the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha for the bhikkhus.”
“It is wonderful, Moggallāna! It is marvelous, Moggallāna!
That this foolish man would wait even until he is seized by the arm!
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks, from this time forward, I shall no longer perform the Uposatha or recite the Pātimokkha.
Monks, you yourselves must henceforth perform the Uposatha and recite the Pātimokkha.
It is impossible, monks, it cannot happen, that the Tathāgata should perform the Uposatha or recite the Pātimokkha with an assembly that is not pure.”
“Monks, there are these eight wonderful and marvelous qualities of the great ocean, seeing which the asuras take delight in the great ocean.
What are the eight?
Monks, the great ocean slopes gradually, inclines gradually, and shelves gradually; it does not fall off with a sheer precipice.”
Furthermore, monks, the great ocean slopes gradually, inclines gradually, and shelves gradually, rather than plunging abruptly;
this, monks, is the first wonderful and marvelous quality of the great ocean, seeing which the asuras take delight in the great ocean.
Furthermore, monks, the great ocean is stable and does not overstep its shore.
Furthermore, monks, the great ocean is stable in its nature and does not overstep its shore.
This, monks, is the second wonderful and marvelous quality of the great ocean, seeing which the asuras take delight in the great ocean.
Furthermore, monks, the great ocean does not dwell with a dead corpse. Whatever dead corpse there is in the great ocean, it quickly carries to the shore and casts up onto the dry land.
Furthermore, monks, the great ocean does not dwell with a dead corpse. Whatever dead corpse there is in the great ocean, it quickly carries to the shore and casts up onto dry land.
This, monks, is the third wonderful and marvelous quality of the great ocean, seeing which the asuras take delight in the great ocean.
Furthermore, monks, whatever great rivers there are—namely, the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Aciravatī, and Sarabhū—[they all flow into the great ocean].
The Mahī, having reached the great ocean, relinquishes its former names and clans and comes to be designated simply as “the great ocean.

And whatever great rivers there are, bhikkhus—namely, the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Aciravatī, Sarabhū, and Mahī—having reached the great ocean, relinquish their former names and clans and come to be designated simply as “the great ocean.
This, bhikkhus, is the fourth astounding and amazing quality of the great ocean, seeing which the asuras take delight in the great ocean.
Furthermore, monks, whatever rivers in the world flow into the great ocean and whatever showers of rain fall from the sky, by these the great ocean is neither seen to diminish nor to be filled.

And because, monks, whatever rivers in the world flow into the great ocean and whatever showers of rain fall from the sky, by these the great ocean is neither seen to diminish nor to be filled; [it remains ever the same].
This, monks, is the fifth wonderful and marvelous quality of the great ocean, seeing which the asuras delight in the great ocean.
Furthermore, monks, the great ocean has a single taste, the taste of salt.
That the great ocean, monks, has a single taste, the taste of salt—
This, monks, is the sixth amazing and wonderful quality of the great ocean, seeing which the asuras take delight in the great ocean.

Furthermore, monks, the great ocean is rich in treasures, possessing many kinds of treasures. These are the treasures therein, namely: pearls, gems, beryl, conch shells, crystal, coral, silver, gold, rubies, and cat's-eye stones.
Furthermore, monks, the great ocean contains many treasures and manifold jewels; these are the jewels, namely: pearls, gems, beryl, conch shells, crystals, coral, silver, gold, rubies, and emeralds.
This, monks, is the seventh wonderful and marvelous quality of the great ocean, which the asuras delight in seeing again and again.
Furthermore, monks, the great ocean is the abode of great beings. These are the beings there: the *timi*, the *timiṅgala*... [and so forth].

Timis, timiṅgalas, asuras, nāgas, and gandhabbas. In the great ocean there are bodies a hundred yojanas long, bodies two hundred yojanas long, bodies three hundred yojanas long, bodies four hundred yojanas long, and bodies five hundred yojanas long.
And because, monks, the great ocean is the abode of great beings, these beings dwell there: timis, timiṅgalas...
The *timitimiṅgala* fish, asuras, nāgas, and gandhabbas— there are in the great ocean bodies a hundred yojanas long,
bodies two hundred yojanas long, and even bodies five hundred yojanas long. This, monks,
is the eighth wonderful and marvelous quality of the great ocean, seeing which the asuras take delight in the great ocean.
“Monks, these are the eight wonderful and marvelous qualities of the great ocean, seeing which the asuras take delight in the great ocean.
In the same way, monks, there are eight wonderful and marvelous qualities in this Dhamma and Discipline, seeing which the bhikkhus take delight in this Dhamma and Discipline.
What are the eight?”
Just as, monks, the great ocean slopes gradually, inclines gradually, and shelves gradually, not falling off with a sheer precipice;
even so, monks, in this Dhamma and Discipline there is gradual training, gradual practice, and gradual progress, and there is no penetration to final knowledge all at once.
And because, monks, in this Dhamma and Discipline there is gradual training, gradual practice, and gradual progress, and no penetration to final knowledge all at once—
This, monks, is the first wonderful and marvelous quality in this Dhamma and Vinaya, seeing which monks take delight in this Dhamma and Vinaya. Just as, monks,
the great ocean is stable in its nature and does not overstep its shore,
even so, monks, whatever training rule has been laid down by me for my disciples, my disciples do not transgress it even for the sake of their lives.

“Monks, even that training rule laid down by me for my disciples which my disciples do not transgress even for the sake of their lives—this, monks, is the second wonderful and marvelous quality in this Dhamma and Vinaya, seeing which the bhikkhus take delight in this Dhamma and Vinaya.
Just as, monks, the great ocean does not dwell together with a dead corpse; whatever dead corpse there is in the great ocean, it quickly carries to the shore and casts up onto the dry land.”
In the same way, monks, that person who is immoral, of evil character, impure, of suspicious conduct, secretive in his actions,
one who is not a recluse yet claims to be a recluse, one who does not lead the holy life yet claims to lead the holy life,
who is inwardly rotten, leaking, and full of filth— the Saṅgha does not dwell together with him; rather, having assembled quickly, they [expel] him.
He is suspended. Even though he may be sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, yet he is far indeed from the Saṅgha, and the Saṅgha is far from him.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, that person who is immoral, of evil nature, impure, of suspect conduct, one whose actions are concealed, a non-recluse claiming to be a recluse, an unchaste man claiming to be chaste, inwardly rotten, leaking, and putrid—
The Saṅgha does not live together with him; having assembled quickly, it suspends him.
Even though he may be seated in the midst of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, yet he is far indeed from the Saṅgha, and the Saṅgha is far from him.
This, monks, is the third wonderful and marvelous quality in this Dhamma and Discipline, seeing which, seeing which, the Bhikkhus take delight in this Dhamma and Discipline.

“Just as, monks, whatever great rivers there are— namely, the Ganges, the Yamunā, the Aciravatī, the Sarabhū, and the Mahī— when they reach the great ocean, they abandon their former names and lineages and are reckoned simply as ‘the great ocean’;
even so, monks, the four castes— the khattiyas, the brāhmaṇas, the vessas, and the suddas—
having gone forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, abandon their former names and lineages and are reckoned simply as ‘recluses.’”
They come to be reckoned simply as ‘Sakyaputtiyas.
Furthermore, monks, when those of the four castes— the khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, and suddas—
go forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, they abandon their former names and clans and become ‘monks.’
They come to be reckoned as "Sakyaputtiyas.
This, monks, is the fourth astounding and amazing quality in this Dhamma and Vinaya, which the bhikkhus, seeing again and again, take delight in this Dhamma and Vinaya.
Just as, monks, whatever rivers in the world flow into the great ocean, and whatever rain falls from the sky, the great ocean is not perceived to become either less or more because of that.
In the same way, monks, even if many bhikkhus attain final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna without residue, no deficiency or fullness is perceived in that element of nibbāna by reason of that.
Monks, because even if many bhikkhus attain final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna without residue, no deficiency or fullness is perceived in that element of nibbāna by reason of that.
This, monks, is the fifth astounding and wonderful quality in this Dhamma and Discipline, seeing which the monks take delight in this Dhamma and Discipline.
Just as, monks, the great ocean has but one taste, the taste of salt, even so, monks, this Dhamma and Discipline has but one taste: the taste of liberation.
“Furthermore, monks, this Dhamma and Discipline has a single flavor, the flavor of liberation.
This, monks, is the sixth astounding and marvelous quality in this Dhamma and Discipline, seeing which the monks take delight in this Dhamma and Discipline.
Just as, monks, the great ocean contains many treasures and manifold treasures, such as these: pearls, gems, beryl, conch shells, crystal, coral, silver, gold, rubies, and cat’s-eye gems;”
In the same way, monks, this Dhamma and Discipline is rich in jewels, possessed of many jewels. These are the jewels therein, namely:
the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.
Moreover, monks, this Dhamma and Vinaya possesses many treasures, manifold treasures; therein these are the treasures, namely:
the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases for psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.
This, monks, is the seventh wonderful and marvelous quality in this Dhamma and Discipline, seeing which the bhikkhus take delight in this Dhamma and Discipline.
Just as, monks, the great ocean is the abode of great beings, such as these beings:
the *timi*, the *timiṅgala*, the *timitimiṅgala*, asuras, nāgas, and gandhabbas; there are in the great ocean bodies a hundred yojanas long, even two hundred yojanas long.
“There are beings with bodies a hundred yojanas long, beings with bodies four hundred yojanas long, and beings with bodies five hundred yojanas long.
In the very same way, monks, this Dhamma and Discipline is the abode of great beings. Therein these are the beings:
the stream-enterer, one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, the once-returner, and one practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning.”
the one practicing, the non-returner, the one practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning, the arahant, and the one practicing for arahantship.
And because, monks, this Dhamma and Vinaya is the abode of great beings, these are the beings therein:
the stream-enterer, the one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, the once-returner, and the one practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning.

One who has entered the path, one who is a non-returner, one who has entered the path for the realization of the fruit of non-returning, one who is an arahant, and one who has entered the path for the attainment of arahantship— this, monks,
is the eighth wonderful and marvelous quality in this Dhamma and Vinaya, seeing which the monks take delight in this Dhamma and Vinaya. These, monks,
are the eight wonderful and marvelous qualities in this Dhamma and Vinaya, seeing which the monks take delight in this Dhamma and Vinaya.”
Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter, on that occasion uttered this inspired exclamation:
“The rain pours down upon what is covered,
but it does not pour down upon what is uncovered.”
Therefore, uncover what is covered;
thus the rain will not soak you. Thus ends the fifth [sutta].
